content.title: Key Takeaways
items: AI Visibility is not something a real estate business can simply "turn on" — it's the ongoing result of making agent, brokerage, location, service, and property-type information clear, consistent, and easy to verify.

No business, tool, or checklist can guarantee that any AI system will recommend, cite, rank, or display a real estate business — AI systems control their own retrieval and ranking mechanisms, entirely outside any individual business's control.

This checklist evaluates 21 categories, from business identity to Fair Housing-conscious content, and should be worked through using observable evidence, not assumptions about what's "probably" already in place.

Fair Housing obligations apply fully to every category touching neighborhoods, buyer/seller targeting, or content framing — this checklist includes a dedicated category for this, and it deserves particular care throughout.
Dynamic real estate information — market statistics, prices, inventory, mortgage rates — must always be sourced, verified, and dated; AI should never be treated as the source of truth for any of it.
The practical sequence for using this checklist is: audit, score, identify gaps, prioritize, improve, verify, and re-audit — a recurring discipline, not a one-time project.

content.content: Prospective buyers and sellers increasingly discover real estate businesses through more than one channel — search engines, Google Maps, directories, reviews, personal websites, and AI-powered search tools. The goal is not to "hack AI." It's to make the business's public information genuinely useful, clear, accurate, and understandable for both people and search systems.

content.title: 2. What Is AI Visibility for a Real Estate Business?
AI Visibility Definition for Real Estate

items.definition: The degree to which a real estate business's publicly available information is clear, consistent, useful, structured, trustworthy, and discoverable enough for search engines and AI-powered systems to potentially understand the business correctly.

content.content: Audit each category in turn, marking items as PASS, PARTIAL, FAIL, or N/A based on observable evidence. Score your audit, prioritize gaps, execute improvements, and re-audit.
Do not mark an item "Pass" based on assumptions. Record observable evidence — specific URLs, screenshots, date checked, and source documents.

content.title: 26. Fair Housing and Responsible Local Content Checklist
Mandatory Fair Housing Compliance Criteria
content.content: Content must avoid steering toward/away from neighborhoods based on protected characteristics, avoid protected-class targeting or demographic assumptions, avoid unsupported safety claims, and ensure neighborhood facts are objective and sourced.

items: Content avoids steering based on protected characteristics
Content avoids protected-class targeting of any kind
Content avoids demographic assumptions
Content avoids unsupported safety claims
Content avoids discriminatory neighborhood descriptions
Neighborhood facts are objective and verifiable
Sources for local claims are documented
Subjective claims are minimized
Potentially sensitive content specifically reviewed for Fair Housing

content.content: The 21 individual category checklists above form the Complete Master Checklist. Review each section methodically against real, observable evidence from your public website and external profiles.

High Readiness (85%+): Information is clear, consistent, and well-maintained. Moderate Readiness (65%–84%): Core foundation present with room for improvement. Needs Improvement (45%–64%): Inconsistencies weaken machine/human understanding. Foundational Gaps (<45%): Major identity, location, or Fair Housing issues require immediate resolution.

rows: Business Identity, NAP Consistency, Fair Housing Compliance
Core Service Pages, Property Type Coverage, Buyer/Seller FAQs
Structured Data, Local Resource Guides, Review Workflows

content.content: A small residential team audits its online presence, finds inconsistent phone numbers across directories, thin buyer FAQ coverage, and an outdated market statistics page, and systematically resolves P1/P2 items to raise its readiness score.

content.title: AI Prompt Template: Real Estate AI Visibility Auditor
content.prompt:
ROLE: You are an expert AI Visibility auditor for real estate businesses.

INPUT: [insert business name, website URL, brokerage info, NAP details, and content summary]

TASK: Evaluate the provided business information against Locatria's 21 AI Visibility categories.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Do not invent facts or assume unverified details.
- Flag any Fair Housing sensitivity (steering, demographic claims).
- Flag un-dated market statistics or inconsistent NAP details.

OUTPUT FORMAT: Categorized diagnostic findings with assigned P1–P4 priorities.

content.title: AI Prompt Template: Real Estate Content Gap Analyzer
content.prompt:
ROLE: You are analyzing a real estate business website for content gaps.

INPUT: [insert list of existing service pages, location pages, and FAQs]

TASK: Identify unaddressed buyer, seller, location, and property-type topics.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Keep all location suggestions objective and factual.
- Do not suggest demographic-based neighborhood descriptions.
- Flag dynamic facts requiring current source verification.

OUTPUT FORMAT: List of Observed Gaps vs. Potential Content Opportunities.

content.title: Real Estate AI Visibility Checklist Questions & Answers

items.question: What is AI Visibility for a real estate business?
items.answer: AI Visibility is how easily and accurately a real estate business's information — identity, location, services, property types, and local expertise — can be discovered and understood across search engines and AI discovery tools.

items.question: Can this checklist guarantee ChatGPT or Google AI visibility?
items.answer: No. AI systems control their own retrieval mechanisms. This checklist optimizes what a business can control: information clarity, consistency, and structure.

items.question: How often should a real estate business perform an audit?
items.answer: At minimum on a recurring quarterly schedule, and immediately following major changes like office relocation, team expansion, or website redesign.

items.question: What Fair Housing risks should be audited?
items.answer: Content must avoid steering, protected-class demographic descriptions, unsupported safety claims, and any language conveying limitation or preference.
